items.snippet:
President Donald Trump has appointed Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy as the interim administrator of NASA, following the withdrawal of Jared Isaacman's nomination. Trump praised Duffy, a former Wisconsin congressman and reality TV star, as a strong temporary leader for NASA. Duffy accepted the role, adding to the list of Trump officials holding multiple positions, such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio also serving as interim national security adviser.

Isaacman's nomination was rescinded in late May just before a Senate vote. Trump cited Isaacman's ties to Elon Musk and alleged Democratic affiliations as reasons for the reversal, despite initial bipartisan donations from Isaacman, who described himself as a right-leaning moderate. In a statement, Isaacman accepted Trump's prerogative to choose his team and expressed support for Duffy as NASA needs trusted political leadership. The events underline the administration’s preference for loyalists in key roles amid Trump's broader reshuffling of senior positions.

items.title: Political chaos leaves France sidelined as investors warm to Europe
items.snippet: France is increasingly sidelined from the investor optimism driving European markets in 2025, due to its political instability and deteriorating public finances. Prime Minister Francois Bayrou's government has faced multiple no-confidence motions and is struggling to identify €40 billion in spending cuts for the 2026 budget. France's budget deficit is now the highest in the eurozone, diverging from neighboring countries that have harnessed inflation to reduce debt. Confidence in French assets has weakened, with investors favoring Italian, German, and Spanish bonds due to France's elevated political and fiscal risks. French stocks also lag behind broader European indices, with the CAC 40 underperforming significantly. Domestically, uncertainty has hurt consumer spending and business activity, while economists have downgraded France's growth forecast amid stagnating economic performance. Public Finances Minister Amélie de Montchalin warned of a potential IMF bailout if fiscal discipline isn't restored, though IMF economist Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas stressed that France must enact substantial spending cuts. With national elections not due until 2027 and few signs of policy stability, investor sentiment remains bleak.

items.title: Spain's Pedro Sánchez fights for his political life
items.snippet: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is confronting the most severe crisis of his premiership amid corruption allegations involving three close aides—Santos Cerdán, José Luís Ábalos, and Koldo García—who are accused of accepting bribes in awarding public construction contracts. Though Sánchez denies knowledge of the wrongdoing and has apologized, the scandal has damaged his credibility and political standing both at home and abroad. Dubbed the "Peugeot gang" by the opposition (PP), the trio once played a central role in Sánchez’s 2016 grassroots campaign. The Socialist party has since distanced itself, branding them a "toxic triangle". The controversy arises just as Sánchez faces international criticism for resisting NATO's demand, spearheaded by Donald Trump, that Spain raise military spending to 5% of GDP. His decision reflects domestic antimilitarism and the fragility of his leftist coalition. Additionally, Sánchez is politically dependent on Catalan separatists for parliamentary support, having agreed to a controversial amnesty law for figures like Carles Puigdemont. This has further alienated EU allies and left him unable to pass legislation. As pressure mounts and public support erodes, Sánchez’s political survival hangs in the balance, with calls intensifying for accountability and reform.
